Fair play

The assistants help you play better, they never cheat for you. Each one sees only what your seat could know: your own cards, the cards shown, every public action, and what follows from those. They never see another player's hidden cards, a face-down card or the order of the cards still to come. Every game is tested for this: two tables that differ only in cards you cannot see must give you the same view and the same advice.

Blackjack

One player against a dealer who follows fixed rules. Basic strategy decides each hand from your cards and the dealer's up card. Counting the cards already shown tells you when the rest of the shoe favours you, and the bet sizing turns that edge into a stake.

The assistant knows
  • your cards, and every hand you hold after a split
  • the dealer's up card and the table rules
  • every card shown since the shuffle: the running count, the true count and what is still unseen
It never sees
  • the dealer's hole card until it is turned over
  • the order of the cards left in the shoe

Expected return by true count

Flat one-unit bets with basic strategy, grouped by the hi-lo true count before the deal. The whiskers are 95% confidence intervals; the dashed line is the weighted fit used for bet sizing below.

Basic strategy

The move for each of your hands (rows) against the dealer's up card (columns), as the assistant plays it. With double after split. Hard totals below 8 always hit and 18 or more always stand.

Bankroll paths: flat betting against Kelly sizing

Hold'em

No-limit Texas hold'em. The assistant deals the cards it cannot see at random from those it has not seen, many times over, to estimate your equity, the share of the pot you would win, and sets that against the price of a call. At the play table the coach also favours hands that fit opponents' public bets. The exhibits below show equity against random hands, the simpler and more optimistic figure.

The assistant knows
  • your hole cards and the board
  • every stack, bet and fold, the button and each move so far
  • which cards are unseen
It never sees
  • anyone else's hole cards before the showdown
  • the burned cards or the cards still to come

Starting-hand equity

Your chance to win (ties split) with each two-card start, all the way to the river, against random hands. Suited hands above the diagonal, offsuit below, pairs on it. More opponents push every hand down.

Pot odds: is the call worth its price?

An opponent bets into a pot. The curve is the equity a call needs to break even, bet ÷ (pot + 2 × bet). Each flat line is the equity of a common flop situation against one random hand: above the curve, calling makes money on average.

GuanDan

A partnership climbing game with 27 cards to each of four players. There is no dealing out of unseen cards here: the assistant splits your own hand into as few plays as it can, and scores each play by how easy it leaves the rest of the hand, adjusted for the trick and how many cards everyone holds.

The assistant knows
  • your hand and the level, so which cards are wild
  • the trick to beat, each seat's card count, every card played and every pass
  • which cards are unseen, wherever they are
It never sees
  • anyone else's hand, your partner's included
  • which seat holds the cards it has not seen

What planning is worth

A team of two planning assistants against a team playing by a simple rule. Each hand is an independent deal at level 2, with a random leader.

What your starting hand is worth

How often your team wins the hand, given what you can read from your own 27 cards before the first play, when all four seats plan. You can see your hand, so you know which column you are in. The dashed line marks a fair share, 50%.

How hands and matches end

The first three tiles split the same hands by where the winner's partner finished, which sets how many levels the team climbs. The others come from whole matches between planners, tribute included.
